title: What records management training must federal agencies provide?
description: 36 CFR 1220.34(f) and NARA Bulletin 2017-01: who needs federal records training, the 60 day and annual deadlines, and the 14 topics, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: US federal agencies must train all personnel on their records management responsibilities under 36 CFR 1220.34(f), issued by the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA). NARA Bulletin 2017-01 sets the detail: everyone who creates, receives, accesses or uses federal records, including contractors and volunteers, completes training within 60 days of employment and an annual refresher, covering 14 minimum topics. Senior officials also receive targeted training on arrival and departure. As at November 2026 the bulletin remains in force.
keyTakeaways: 36 CFR 1220.34(f) requires each agency to "provide guidance and training to all agency personnel on their records management responsibilities, including identification of Federal records, in all formats and media."

NARA Bulletin 2017-01, Agency Records Management Training Requirements, dated November 29, 2016, applies to federal employees, contractors, volunteers and others who create, receive, access or use federal records on behalf of the agency.
Initial training is due within 60 days of employment, followed by annual refresher training.
Political appointees, senior agency officials and senior executives receive targeted training on arrival and departure, and within three to six months before a presidential administration change.
Training must cover 14 minimum topics, including email and electronic messages, legal holds, departing employees, and what to do when records are lost or destroyed without authorization.
appliesTo: Federal executive branch agencies subject to the Federal Records Act and NARA regulations in 36 CFR Chapter XII, Subchapter B
Federal employees who create, receive, access or use federal records
Contractors, volunteers and others who handle federal records on behalf of an agency
Political appointees, senior agency officials and senior executives (targeted training)

blocks.text: Section 1220.34 lists the core responsibilities of every agency records management program, and paragraph (f) makes training one of them. The other paragraphs require agencies to designate a records officer, issue directives, assign records duties, build records requirements into electronic systems, schedule all records for NARA approval and evaluate their programs.

blocks.title: 36 CFR 1220.34(f)
blocks.text: "Provide guidance and training to all agency personnel on their records management responsibilities, including identification of Federal records, in all formats and media."

The regulation sets the obligation but not the timing or content. NARA filled that gap with Bulletin 2017-01, issued under the authority of 36 CFR 1220.34, OMB Circular A-130 and two joint OMB and NARA memoranda on managing government records (M-12-18 and M-14-16). The bulletin states that it expires when revoked or superseded.

sections.heading: Who must complete records management training?

blocks.text: Everyone who handles federal records for the agency, not only federal employees. The bulletin says it "applies to all agency personnel, which includes Federal employees, contractors, volunteers and others that create, receive, access, or use Federal records on behalf of the agency."

The contractor coverage matters for the private sector. Under the bulletin's definition, contractor staff who handle agency records fall within the same 60 day and annual training cycle as employees, so contractor onboarding plans should allow for it. Contractors in defense work often face this alongside [CUI training](/regulations/cui-training-requirements) and [federal cybersecurity awareness training](/regulations/federal-employee-cybersecurity-awareness-training).

sections.heading: When must records management training be completed?

blocks.text: Initial training is due within 60 days of employment and must be refreshed every year. Senior officials have additional event-driven training.

blocks.text: Because both deadlines run from individual events, tracking by employment start date rather than by calendar campaign is the reliable approach. See [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

sections.heading: What topics must records management training cover?

blocks.text: The bulletin sets 14 minimum content areas. Agencies may add agency-specific material, but each of these must appear.

items: Describe how records management supports the agency's mission and business processes, and public access to government information.
Give an overview of government-wide and agency-specific records management policies and recordkeeping requirements.
Explain legal responsibilities for creating, maintaining and disposing of federal records.
Describe the records lifecycle, including the difference between temporary and permanent records.
Distinguish records from nonrecord and personal materials.
Describe how records are maintained and filed in the agency.
Explain how legal holds and the discovery phase of litigation affect records handling, retention and disposition.
Describe how and where to store agency federal records.
Describe how agency information technology systems are used for records management.
Describe how to manage record and nonrecord materials in email, social media and other electronic messages.
Describe what to do with records and nonrecord materials when an employee leaves the agency.
Describe what to do when records are removed, lost or destroyed without proper authorization.
Describe where to get more information about records management.

blocks.text: Topic 11 has a statutory edge. Under [44 U.S.C. 2911](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/44/2911), an executive agency employee who creates or sends a record from a non-official electronic messaging account must copy an official account at the time or forward a complete copy to an official account "not later than 20 days after the original creation or transmission of the record." An intentional violation is a basis for disciplinary action.

sections.heading: How should agencies evidence records management training?

blocks.text: Neither the regulation nor the bulletin prescribes a form of evidence, so agencies should keep records that prove each person met each deadline and that the content covered every required topic. A completion list without dates or content versions cannot show either.

items: **Population:** a roster that includes contractors and volunteers, not only staff in the HR system.
**Timeliness:** employment start date against first completion, to show the 60 day window.
**Coverage:** a mapping from the course to the 14 topics, kept with each course version.
**Senior officials:** separate logs for arrival, departure and pre-transition briefings.
**Program evaluation:** 36 CFR 1220.34(j) requires agencies to conduct formal evaluations of their records programs, and training records are part of what an evaluation examines.

blocks.text: Training records are themselves federal records and need a disposition schedule. For retention thinking, see [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records), and for structure, [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry treats each of the 14 required topics as a defined learning outcome linked to the agency's own records policies, file plans and schedules, so coverage of every topic is visible for each course version. Role and event triggers, such as arrival, departure or an administration change, are modeled alongside the annual cycle. Agency use cases are described on the [government and defense page](/industries/government-defence).

faqs.q: Do contractors have to complete federal records management training?
faqs.a: Yes, where they create, receive, access or use federal records on behalf of the agency. NARA Bulletin 2017-01 defines agency personnel to include contractors and volunteers, so the 60 day initial training and annual refresher apply to them on the same terms as employees. The agency usually delivers the course and records completion.

faqs.q: Can an agency use NARA's own training materials?
faqs.a: The bulletin sets content and timing but does not require a particular course, so agencies may build their own or adapt available material, provided every one of the 14 minimum topics is covered and agency-specific policies, file plans and contacts are included. Generic content alone will not cover topics such as how records are filed in that agency.

faqs.q: Is records management training the same as cybersecurity or privacy training?
faqs.a: No. Records management training is a separate obligation under 36 CFR 1220.34(f), focused on identifying, keeping and disposing of federal records. Agencies often schedule it alongside annual information security awareness training, but combining delivery does not remove the need to cover all 14 records topics and to evidence them separately.

faqs.q: What happens if an employee mishandles records after training?
faqs.a: Topic 13 requires training on what to do when records are removed, lost or destroyed without authorization, because 36 CFR 1230.14 requires agencies to report promptly any unlawful or accidental removal, defacing, alteration or destruction of records to NARA. For electronic messages sent from personal accounts, 44 U.S.C. 2911 makes an intentional failure to copy or forward the record within 20 days a basis for disciplinary action.
